title: Support for political reform can coexist with low confidence that reform is achievable
source_unit: Pew Research Center analysis of recent U.S. public-opinion surveys and Congress.gov amendment records

observations.period: 2025 survey referenced in Pew's July 2026 analysis

denominator.unit: percent of U.S. adults in the referenced Pew survey

major_or_complete_reform_needed.unit: percent saying the political system needs major changes or complete reform

confident_change_can_happen.unit: percent confident that major political change can happen

pessimistic_reformers.unit: share saying major or complete reform is needed while lacking confidence it can happen

observations.method: Pew analysis of a prior U.S. public-opinion survey; the combined pessimistic-reformer category is a descriptive intersection of reform judgment and perceived feasibility.
observations.uncertainty: The article summarizes the referenced survey rather than presenting a full new microdata release here. The measures do not show which reforms respondents prefer, whether they coordinate around them, or whether confidence changes after a political event.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults; the source's headline comparison is national and does not establish a single shared reform program across parties.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low confidence may reflect constitutional difficulty, current partisan conflict, distrust of institutions, or realistic assessment of political barriers; it does not necessarily mean apathy or rejection of democratic institutions.

denominator.unit: percent of U.S. adults in the cited Pew surveys

congressional_term_limits_2023.unit: percent favoring limits on the number of terms members of Congress can serve

federal_official_age_limits_2023.unit: percent favoring a maximum age limit for federal elected officials

campaign_spending_limits_2024.unit: percent favoring limits on political campaign spending

popular_vote_president_2024.unit: percent preferring the candidate with the most votes to win the presidency

observations.method: Descriptive summaries of separate Pew surveys conducted in different years; the reform items are not treated as one simultaneous ballot or unified policy package.
observations.uncertainty: Question wording, dates, partisan divisions, and constitutional requirements differ across proposals. Support for an abstract reform does not establish knowledge of implementation details, durable intensity, or willingness to bear political cost.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults; the source reports some partisan comparisons, including a larger partisan split on direct presidential popular vote than on several other reforms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Broad support can reflect dissatisfaction with incumbents or general anti-corruption sentiment rather than agreement on institutional design; constitutional barriers can separate opinion from enactment.

related_sources.claim: The constitutional amendment route imposes a formal feasibility barrier distinct from public support.

boundary: This record identifies a gap between public demand for political change and confidence that change is possible. It does not establish reform action, coordination, turnout, protest, institutional performance, causal polarization, or successful constitutional change.
